I am 74 years old and have been farming this same land in Quzhou for 55 years. My bones know the rhythm of this plain: winter wheat, summer maize, on the same 6 mu, year after year. I only finished primary school, but I have seen enough seasons to know what works and what does not. My household has four mouths, and some of the younger ones work off-farm in town, so I cannot afford to take risks or try anything fancy. I need a rotation that is predictable, that the grain station will buy, and that I can manage mostly by myself.

For wheat, I will plant an improved variety — probably Jimai or something similar from the county seed co-op — in early October. I will run the rotary tiller after the maize stalks are cleared to break up the ground and bury the residue. Wheat needs water, especially in spring, so I will run the pump three times: once before winter to help it settle, once at greening, and once at jointing. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and top-dress with urea when the wheat starts growing again. I also spray for weeds and aphids — usually three times through the season. I expect around 450 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

For maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in June. At my age, with less help at home, I do not plough for maize anymore — I direct-seed into the wheat stubble. It saves diesel, time, and my back. I use hybrid seed, usually Denghai, because it gives good yield and I know how it behaves. Summer rains usually carry the maize, but I will irrigate twice if July turns dry, especially during silking. I fertilize at planting and maybe once more if the leaves look pale. Two pesticide sprays are enough — one for weeds and one for corn borer if I see it. I expect about 550 kg per mu.

I do not change what has worked for three generations. The wheat floor price gives me security, and the maize pays for the inputs.
